約伊希科弓琴是來自芬蘭與卡累利阿的傳統弓奏里拉琴，通常有兩或三條弦，傳統以馬毛製: The jouhikko is a traditional bowed lyre from Finland and Karelia, usually with two or three strings, traditionally of horsehair, a chordophone, H-S number 321.22. It has no fingerboard: the player puts a hand through a hole in the soundboard and stops the melody string with the backs of the fingers, while another string sounds as a drone, and the range is mostly six notes. The instrument was traditionally used for dance tunes, was lost for a time in the early 20th century, and was revived by folk-music collecting and by modern ensembles.
約伊希科弓琴為芬蘭與卡累利阿傳統弓奏里拉。最早明確描繪之一見於14世紀第二季挪威: The jouhikko is a traditional bowed lyre of Finland and Karelia. One of the earliest clear depictions is a stone carving of the second quarter of the 14th century in Trondheim Cathedral in Norway; 18th-century Latin writers mention a similar instrument, and the first illustration appeared around 1830. Related bowed lyres are distributed from Russia through Scandinavia to Britain and Ireland. From the late 19th century to the early 20th, folk-music collectors recorded players, instruments, tunes and sound recordings, and A. O. Väisänen collected tunes between 1913 and 1931. Playing declined in the early 20th century and later revived; modern instruments use horsehair, nylon, gut or viola metal strings, and under the influence of the Estonian talharpa the hand hole has been enlarged and the playing method adjusted.
